summary: MPLS networks have many MIB modules for management, each in its own document. This informational RFC gives an overview of the MIB modules used to manage the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) and how they fit together.

plainLanguage.summary: Many different instruction booklets exist for running one machine. This is the table of contents saying which booklet to read.

questions: which mibs are used to manage mpls-tp
how do you manage mpls-tp networks
what mib modules exist for mpls
subtitle: Organizing management tools for carrier-grade packet networks

tldr.problem: MPLS-TP (Multiprotocol Label Switching Transport Profile) networks need to be managed reliably, but the necessary management information base (MIB) modules exist in many separate documents and fit together in unclear ways.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC maps out which existing MPLS and pseudowire MIB modules apply to MPLS-TP, identifies gaps where new modules are needed, and recommends the structure of additional MIBs for operations, alarms, protection switching, and other functions.
tldr.outcome: Network operators gain a clear roadmap for implementing SNMP-based management of MPLS-TP networks, knowing which existing tools to reuse and where to build new ones.

today: RFC 6639 is Informational and remains the definitive overview of MPLS-TP MIB-based management architecture. It was written as an overview and reference guide; work on individual MIB modules has continued in other RFCs.

sections.title: What is MPLS-TP?
sections.content:
MPLS-TP is a version of Multiprotocol Label Switching designed specifically for carriers who run packet-switched transport networks. Unlike general-purpose MPLS, MPLS-TP is optimized for the high reliability, deterministic behavior, and static provisioning that carriers need in their backbones.

Managing MPLS-TP networks requires monitoring and controlling many elements: the logical paths that packets follow (called Label Switched Paths or LSPs), virtual circuits that emulate legacy services (pseudowires), fault detection, performance measurement, and protection switching (automatic failover when a link breaks). The IETF has defined numerous MIB modules (management information bases, which are data structures accessed via SNMP) to describe these elements, but they are scattered across many documents.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS-TP is MPLS tuned up for telephone company networks. Managing it means keeping track of many moving parts, and the instructions for doing that are spread across many documents.

sections.title: The Existing MIB Module Ecosystem
sections.content:
The IETF has already published MIB modules for the core MPLS functions that MPLS-TP uses. These include modules for textual conventions (shared data types), label switched routers (the devices that forward labeled packets), label edge routers (devices that add and remove labels), traffic engineering, pseudowires, protection switching, and fast reroute (automatic backup paths). Each module focuses on a specific aspect and is defined in a separate RFC.

These modules are organized in a hierarchy with dependencies: textual convention modules define data types used everywhere, core modules build on those, and optional modules extend functionality. The document maps this entire forest so operators understand which modules are prerequisites for others.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF has already written instruction booklets for most of the pieces. This document is a map showing which booklets you need to read first and how they connect.

sections.title: Gaps Between MPLS and MPLS-TP
sections.content:
When operators try to apply the existing MPLS MIB modules to MPLS-TP, they find several gaps. MPLS-TP networks can be identified by special identifiers (Global_ID and Node_ID) that the existing MPLS modules do not support. MPLS-TP also requires bidirectional tunnels where traffic flows in both directions along the same path, a setup that the current MIB modules do not fully model. In some environments (particularly outside the traditional Internet), the modules also lack support for identification schemes used by telephone carriers.

For Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM), MPLS-TP adds functions like continuity checking, remote defect indication, and packet loss measurement that existing modules do not cover. Protection switching in MPLS-TP includes linear, ring, and mesh topologies, and the modules need extensions for each. Interface management and the concept of MPLS-TP "sections" (link-level paths) also require new tools.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS-TP works a bit differently than regular MPLS. The management booklets don't cover paths that go both directions, special ID schemes, health checks, or automatic rerouting in ring networks.

sections.title: New MIB Modules Required
sections.content:
The document recommends creating new MIB modules in several categories. For the core MPLS-TP data plane, new modules should define textual conventions (shared data types) and identifiers, extend the label switching router (LSR) module for bidirectional paths, and extend the traffic engineering tunnel module for MPLS-TP-specific attributes. For pseudowires (virtual circuits), similar extensions are needed.

For OAM, two major modules are recommended: one extending the existing BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) module for use on MPLS LSPs and pseudowires, and another defining maintenance points and entity groups that form the OAM hierarchy. For protection switching, three modules are proposed covering linear (1:1 or 1:N), ring, and mesh protection topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: New instruction booklets are needed for: making labels go both ways, managing health checks, defining what to do when a link breaks in different network shapes, and virtual circuits on MPLS-TP.

sections.title: The Management Architecture
sections.content:
MPLS-TP management uses SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), the standard way that network operators query and configure devices. The management function separates into five main areas: fault management (detecting problems), configuration management (setting up paths), performance monitoring (measuring traffic), accounting (tracking usage), and security management (controlling access). This separation means operators can manage MPLS-TP networks independently of whatever client networks (IP, Ethernet, or others) run on top of them.

The document does not mandate a single preferred management approach but describes how the MIB modules should fit together so that management systems can query devices systematically. It emphasizes that the modules should be compliant with SMIv2 (the data definition language for MIBs) and that textual conventions should be imported consistently across modules to ensure interoperability between vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is the standard way to manage networks. The modules should fit together so a management system can ask a device what it knows and tell it what to do, no matter which vendor built the device.
